status_summary: Kratom and its alkaloids mitragynine and 7-OH are Schedule I controlled substances under Alabama law (Ala. Code 20-2-23, in force since 2016), per LAPPA. Gov. Kay Ivey and ALEA said on 2026-09-30 that kratom is illegal in Alabama and that Operation Southern Shield, launched in May, has executed 83 search warrants and seized nearly 123,000 doses.
seven_oh_rule: Covered: mitragynine and 7-OH are Schedule I with no threshold
pending: none found

status_summary: LAPPA's January 2026 summary lists no Alaska statute or regulation on kratom. The Anchorage Assembly Public Safety Committee reviewed a draft municipal ordinance on 2026-10-07, according to the Anchorage Daily News.
seven_oh_rule: none
local_action: Anchorage: draft ordinance (sponsor Janice Park) would make recreational sale, possession or use of concentrated 7-OH and products marketed as kratom analogues a Class B misdemeanor, exempting kratom in unaltered form; Assembly introduction was expected 2026-10-20 (outcome not confirmed)
pending: Anchorage ordinance introduction/vote not confirmed; no statewide bill found

status_summary: Arizona's 2019 Kratom Consumer Protection Act (A.R.S. 36-795 to 36-795.03) bars sales to under-18s, caps 7-OH at 2 percent of alkaloids, bans synthetic alkaloids and requires mitragynine/7-OH labeling, per LAPPA. HB 2415, which would have raised the age to 21 and tightened rules, passed both chambers in different forms but the legislature's record shows no governor action or chapter number. Attorney General Kris Mayes sued Botanic Tonics under the Consumer Fraud Act on 2026-09-23.
seven_oh_rule: Statute caps 7-OH at 2 percent of alkaloid fraction and bans synthetic 7-OH and synthetic mitragynine
pending: none found

status_summary: Mitragynine and 7-OH are Schedule I controlled substances in Arkansas (Arkansas Department of Health list; Ark. Admin. Code 007.07.2), per LAPPA. NEA Report said on 2026-11-06 that a Jonesboro gas station owner faces a Class C felony possession charge after Arkansas Regulatory Police found 62 suspected kratom pills on 2026-11-05.
seven_oh_rule: Covered: 7-OH is Schedule I
pending: none found (Jonesboro defendant's first court date reported as Jan. 25, year not stated)

status_summary: California has no kratom-specific statute. The Department of Public Health treats kratom and 7-OH products for consumption as illegal to sell under existing food law, and Gov. Gavin Newsom's office reported on 2026-09-02 that 7,888 kratom/7-OH products were removed from shelves in 8,038 site visits, with 97.75 percent compliance among ABC licensees. Basis is agency enforcement rather than a scheduling statute; classification is a judgment call.
seven_oh_rule: Treated together with kratom as prohibited for consumption; AB 1088 would have capped 7-OH at 2 percent of alkaloids
local_action: Fountain Valley: council voted 4-1 on 2026-07-15 to ban products above 2 percent 7-OH, 21+ limit (LA Times). Blythe: under-21 sales ban took effect 2026-09-10. San Mateo County: countywide ban reported by SF Chronicle (date not confirmed). Downey: staff told 2026-09-08 to draft 7-OH ordinance. La Habra weighing a ban.
pending: AB 1088 (2 percent 7-OH cap, product rules) is a two-year bill; trackers conflict and the official leginfo page could not be opened, so final status not confirmed; no sources show it enacted

status_summary: Colorado regulates kratom under the Daniel Bregger Act (SB 25-072): 21+ sales, labeling, display limits, a 7-OH cap of 2 percent of total alkaloids and a ban on synthetic alkaloids, per LAPPA and the attorney general. AG Phil Weiser announced a $152,000 settlement on 2026-09-21 with a 15-shop chain accused of exceeding the 7-OH limit.
seven_oh_rule: Cap of 2 percent of total alkaloids; synthetic alkaloids prohibited
local_action: Castle Rock: town council voted 6-1 on 2026-10-06 for final passage of a retail kratom sales ban (fine up to $2,650, up to a year in jail; possession not banned), effective November 2026 (exact day not confirmed), per Denver7 and Castle Rock News-Press.
pending: none found

status_summary: Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa, leaves, stems and extracts) and 7-OH are Schedule I controlled substances in Connecticut; the regulations received final approval on 2026-04-02 and are in effect, per the Department of Consumer Protection. Wallingford police arrested two PuffCity employees in September over a product containing 7-OH, the Hartford Courant reported.
seven_oh_rule: Covered: 7-OH and kratom Schedule I
pending: none found

status_summary: Gov. Matt Meyer signed HS 1 for HB 332 on 2026-09-08, effective the same day: selling, providing or marketing kratom to anyone under 21 is a class B misdemeanor, per the General Assembly's bill record. The bill as signed does not ban synthetic products or require alkaloid labeling.
seven_oh_rule: none
pending: DATE and DHSS must report to the governor and General Assembly on testing capability and retailer licensing by 2027-01-01

status_summary: DC regulation (22-B DCMR 1201) lists 7-hydroxymitragynine in Schedule I; DC statute does not list kratom, mitragynine or 7-OH, and LAPPA calls the legal status of natural leaf unclear (January 2026). No 2026 DC action found.
seven_oh_rule: 7-OH Schedule I by regulation since 2016; kratom leaf and mitragynine not addressed
pending: none found

status_summary: Florida sets a 21+ limit for kratom products (Fla. Stat. 500.92, misdemeanor). Attorney General James Uthmeier's emergency rule 2ER26-2 (effective 2026-08-18, superseding 2ER26-1 of 2026-06-22) places 7-OH above 1 mg/g or 1 mg/mL, or with under 100:1 mitragynine-to-7-OH ratio, plus related compounds, in Schedule I; the Department of Agriculture issued emergency labeling rule 5KER26-11 requiring 7-OH disclosure. Natural leaf is not scheduled.
seven_oh_rule: Schedule I by emergency rule above 1,000 ppm or ratio under 100:1; MGM-15, MGM-16, 7-acetoxymitragynine and others listed
local_action: Leon County: commissioners voted 2026-10-13 to draft an ordinance banning certain derivatives, back before the board Nov. 17; Sarasota and Liberty counties have adopted ordinances (per WCTV)
pending: Emergency rule 2ER26-2 expiry date not confirmed (flrules.org lists none; 2026 legislature did not codify per KNT coverage); Leon County ordinance Nov. 17

status_summary: Georgia's Kratom Consumer Protection Act (HB 181, signed 2024-05-02, effective 2025-01-01) requires 21+, behind-the-counter or secured display, labeling, and caps products at 150 mg mitragynine and 1 mg 7-OH per serving and 0.5 mg 7-OH per gram, and bans synthetic alkaloids. Correction to June edition: HB 181 is the 2024 law, not a 2026 enactment effective July 1, 2026. Attorney General Chris Carr asked lawmakers on 2026-10-15 for a default-ban law.
seven_oh_rule: Cap 0.5 mg/g and 1 mg per serving; synthetic 7-OH and mitragynine banned
local_action: Fulton County commissioners backed a resolution 2026-09-17 to ban synthetic kratom and put natural kratom behind pharmacy counters (legal force unclear); Franklin County drafting ban on kratom-derived products in convenience stores; Hart County leading regional effort
pending: House Blue-Ribbon Study Committee on kratom met June 17 and Aug 21; recommendations and 2027 session action pending

status_summary: LAPPA's January 2026 summary lists no Hawaii kratom statute; Hawaii's kratom regulation bills (SB 463/HB 717) did not become law. The Department of Law Enforcement posted a Notice of Emergency Controlled Substance Scheduling Action on 2026-11-05 covering 7-OH, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15, citing HRS 329-11(e); it requires 30 days' public notice before taking effect.
seven_oh_rule: Emergency Schedule I listing of 7-OH, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15 posted 2026-11-05, not yet in force as of 2026-11-09 under the 30-day notice rule; threshold not read
pending: Emergency scheduling effective about 2026-12-05 (30 days after posting; exact date not confirmed); lapses unless 2027 session enacts, per HRS 329-11(e)

status_summary: Idaho has no statewide kratom law; the 2026 legislature considered regulation bills (SB 1282, SB 1418) but none passed, per CBS2 and LAPPA. Cities are acting: Idaho Falls banned sales effective 2026-07-01, Coeur d'Alene adopted a permit, 21+ and 7-OH cap ordinance on 2026-09-15, and Pocatello's council directed staff on 2026-11-06 to proceed with a sales-ban ordinance.
seven_oh_rule: none statewide; Coeur d'Alene caps 7-OH at 2 percent and 1 mg per serving
local_action: Idaho Falls sales ban effective 2026-07-01 (possession not banned); Coeur d'Alene permit/21+/7-OH cap ordinance adopted 2026-09-15 (Coeur d'Alene Press); Pocatello sales ban in progress, council consideration expected 2026-11-19 per city notice
pending: Pocatello ordinance vote expected 2026-11-19; Coeur d'Alene license fee still to be set

status_summary: Illinois has no statewide kratom ban or 7-OH rule. Under the Kratom Control Act (720 ILCS 642/5), as summarized by the Legislative Analysis and Public Policy Association (January 2026), selling kratom to anyone under 18 is a Class B misdemeanor; kratom is not a controlled substance.
seven_oh_rule: none
local_action: Naperville council voted 8-0 on 2026-09-02 to ban retail sales of natural and synthetic kratom effective 2026-10-01 (Chicago Tribune via KNT); Streator council approved a synthetic-kratom ban with concentration limits on 2026-10-21 while leaving natural leaf for adults 21+ (Shaw Local); Effingham County Board unanimously approved a countywide ban on kratom, phenibut and 7-OH sales the week of 2026-10-21 (WCIA); Wilmington council adopted a ban on kratom and 7-OH sales on 2026-11-04 (Shaw Local); Mount Carmel and Peru councils moved toward synthetic-kratom bans (outcomes not confirmed)
pending: Statewide bills stalled: HB 4737 (Kratom Consumer Protection Act, 2% 7-OH cap, age 21) re-referred to Rules 2026-03-27; SB 3160 (Kratom Prohibition Act) sent to committee 2026-02-18; no 2027 filings found

status_summary: Per the Legislative Analysis and Public Policy Association (January 2026), mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine have been listed as synthetic drugs, and so Schedule I controlled substances, in Indiana since 2012 (Ind. Code 35-31.5-2-321 and 35-48-2-4). KNT found no 2026 change.
seven_oh_rule: Mitragynine and 7-OH both covered by the same Schedule I listing
pending: none found

status_summary: Iowa has no statewide kratom law. Gov. Kim Reynolds called for a total ban on kratom and synthetic variants on 2026-09-01, citing 45 kratom-associated deaths since 2024, per the state HHS release; a Senate regulation bill died without a floor vote earlier this year (KNT, citing Iowa Capital Dispatch).
seven_oh_rule: none
pending: Governor's call for a total ban; ban bills (HF 2133, SF 2013) and a regulation bill (HF 612) were introduced in the 91st General Assembly and not enacted; 2027 pre-filings none found

status_summary: Kansas House Bill 2365 places 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) in Schedule I, and the enrolled bill takes effect on publication in the statute book, which KNT-cited coverage dates to 2026-07-01. The enrolled text does not name mitragynine or kratom leaf, though some coverage describes the law as a ban on kratom and 7-OH.
seven_oh_rule: 7-OH listed in Schedule I (K.S.A. 65-4105 as amended by HB 2365); mitragynine not named in the enrolled bill
local_action: Lawrence and Johnson County issued enforcement and resource notices ahead of 2026-07-01 (KNT, citing Lawrence Journal-World and Johnson County)
pending: none found

status_summary: Kentucky regulates kratom products under KRS 217.2201 to 217.2209 (effective 2024-07-15), with an under-21 sales ban, labeling and a 7-OH cap. A Cabinet for Health and Family Services regulation (902 KAR 55:015, filed with the Legislative Research Commission 2026-01-09) lists 7-OH above 400 parts per million as Schedule I and states the listing does not apply to mitragynine.
seven_oh_rule: 7-OH above 400 ppm (dry weight) is Schedule I; kratom products may not exceed a 7-OH cap in the alkaloid fraction (KRS 217.2202)
pending: Amended KRS 217.2202 provisions take effect 2027-07-01 per the Kentucky Revised Statutes chapter index (2026 Acts ch. 198); 2027 session: HB 9 taxation and licensing note mentions kratom (not confirmed, from search only)

status_summary: Kratom, mitragynine and 7-OH are Schedule I under Act 41 of 2025 (La. R.S. 40:966.1), effective 2025-08-01, per the Legislative Analysis and Public Policy Association. On 2026-10-19 the Louisiana Department of Health issued an emergency rule adding mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15 and MGM-16 to Schedule I, mirroring the DEA's temporary federal listing (WDSU; KNT, citing the LDH release).
seven_oh_rule: Mitragynine and 7-OH Schedule I by statute; MGM-15, MGM-16 and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl added by emergency rule LAC 46:LIII.2704
minimum_age: 21 (sale to under 21 unlawful, La. R.S. 14:91.10; moot under the ban)
pending: Emergency rule stays in force for the maximum period allowed under the state Administrative Procedure Act or until a final rule is adopted (KNT, citing LDH; LDH page returned 403 to us)

status_summary: Maine has no statewide kratom-specific law, per the Legislative Analysis and Public Policy Association (January 2026). KNT and a web search found no 2026 enactment.
seven_oh_rule: none
pending: none found

status_summary: Maryland's Kratom Consumer Protection Act (Health-General 21-2E-01 to 21-2E-04, effective 2024-10-01) bars sales to under-21s, adulterated or synthetic-alkaloid products and products with more than 2% 7-OH in the alkaloid fraction, and requires mitragynine and 7-OH labeling. Chapters 354 and 355 of 2026 (HB 1523, SB 820) add Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission seizure and enforcement powers over unauthorized consumable products, including products with more than 1 mg of 7-OH per serving.
seven_oh_rule: 2% of alkaloid fraction cap for kratom products; 1 mg per serving cap for other 7-OH products; synthetic alkaloids barred
local_action: City of Baltimore sued three kratom sellers under its consumer protection ordinance (removed to federal court 2026-09-01; sellers moved to dismiss, Law360 via KNT)
pending: none found

status_summary: Under an emergency regulation (105 CMR 726.000) issued by Public Health Commissioner Robbie Goldstein on 2026-08-13 and effective 2026-08-28, all forms of kratom are temporarily Schedule I in Massachusetts for up to a year, covering natural leaf as well as concentrated and synthetic 7-OH, per the Governor's office and town notices.
seven_oh_rule: All 7-OH covered by the all-kratom Schedule I order
minimum_age: none (all sales illegal without a controlled-substances registration)
local_action: More than 25 communities adopted local bans (Arlington 2026-08-19, Deerfield 2026-08-13, Burlington 2026-09, Hopkinton, Tisbury, Edgartown 2026-06-09); Springfield sent 500+ notices and is weighing a trigger ordinance for when the state order lapses; Lynnfield upheld $3,000 fines (KNT)
pending: Four retailers' suit in Suffolk Superior Court was pending with no hearing scheduled as of WBUR's 2026-09-10 report; order runs up to one year (to about 2027-08); House Ways and Means bill on synthetic kratom and 7-OH above 2% pending

status_summary: Michigan has no statewide kratom law in force. House Bill 5537, a ban on kratom and synthetic variants including 7-OH, passed the House 56-48 on 2026-03-18 and sits in the Senate Government Operations Committee; Rep. Bryan DeBoyer is pushing for Senate passage before year end (Fox 17 via KNT).
seven_oh_rule: none in force; HB 5537 would ban 7-OH as a synthetic variant
local_action: Warren council approved first reading of a sales ban (2026-07); Canton Township advanced a 21+ and 500-foot-buffer ordinance (2026-09-08); Plymouth Township advanced a township-wide sales ban (2026-10-13, final vote set for 2026-10-27, outcome not confirmed) (KNT)
pending: HB 5537 pending in Senate (Senate returns 2026-11-12); separate SB 1181 Kratom Consumer Protection Act bill (not confirmed, from search only); June edition said the House vote was in May, the bill page shows March

status_summary: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. 152.027 subd. 7, amended by 2026 Laws ch. 63) makes selling kratom or mitragynine or 7-OH products to anyone under 21 a gross misdemeanor, up from 18; the revisor's page shows the 2026 amendment. KFF Health News reported the new age limit on 2026-08-04.
seven_oh_rule: none
pending: A Schedule II classification was floated in the 2026 session and did not pass (KNT, citing FOX 9); 2027 bills none found

status_summary: Mississippi regulates kratom products under HB 1077 of 2025 (Miss. Code 75-103-1 to 75-103-7, effective 2025-07-01): sales to under-21s are barred, products go behind the counter, and a lawful product may hold 7-OH at no more than 1% of total alkaloids and 0.5 mg per container. A 25% excise tax applies. The Attorney General, Lt. Gov. and State Health Officer have called for a statewide ban in 2027 (KNT).
seven_oh_rule: 7-OH capped at 1% of alkaloids and 0.5 mg per container; synthesized alkaloids barred
local_action: Tupelo (ordinance 2026-02-03, enforced 2026-09-12), Guntown and Saltillo bans; Lee County ban effective 2026-09-16; Hattiesburg draft ordinance discussed 2026-11-02 (KNT, citing WTVA, WDAM)
pending: House Drug Policy Committee heard testimony 2026-11-04 toward 2027 ban or tighter regulation; AG Fitch, Lt. Gov. Hosemann, State Health Officer Edney and the state medical association back an all-kratom ban; Rep. Yancey synthetic-kratom bill

status_summary: Missouri adopted the DEA's temporary Schedule I listing of mitragynine pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15 on 2026-09-25, and Attorney General Catherine Hanaway says products with artificially elevated 7-OH are Schedule I analogues. Her office has issued 31 civil investigative demands and cease-and-desist letters. There is no statewide leaf framework.
seven_oh_rule: MGM-15 and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl Schedule I (adopted 2026-09-25); AG treats concentrated or added 7-OH as an analogue
local_action: Kansas City ordinance (2026-02) bans synthetic kratom and requires a license and age 21; Jackson County legislature held a 7-OH and kratom sales ordinance on 2026-10-26 (Fox 4 via KNT)
pending: Jackson County ordinance expected within weeks; litigation and AG enforcement ongoing; 2027 bills none found

status_summary: Montana has no statewide kratom law; several 2025 bills did not pass, per the Daily Montanan. The Law and Justice Interim Committee tabled a Kratom Consumer Protection Act 8-1 on 2026-09-01, while the Economic Affairs Interim Committee advanced a draft bill to schedule kratom compounds.
seven_oh_rule: none
local_action: Missoula City-County Health Department bars kratom food and drink products from licensed retail food businesses after 2026-11-02; Yellowstone County's RiverStone Health began the same enforcement in January and sued four businesses in May (Montana Free Press via KNT)
pending: Interim-committee ban draft and regulation bill head to the 2027 session

status_summary: Nebraska's Kratom Consumer Protection Act (LB230, 2025, amended by LB901, 2026; operative date of the 2026 amendments July 18, 2026) bars sales to anyone under 21, requires age verification online, requires state product registration with the Department of Revenue, and bans products with synthesized alkaloids, per the Nebraska Legislature statute text.
seven_oh_rule: Product is not a lawful 'kratom product' if it has synthesized alkaloids or 7-OH above 2% of the alkaloid fraction; combustible, vaporized and injectable forms excluded
pending: Product-registration list to start on an implementation date set by the Tax Commissioner (date not confirmed)

status_summary: Nevada's Kratom Consumer Protection Act, NRS 597.998 (added 2019), bars knowing sales to anyone under 18, bars adulterated kratom, requires a label with ingredients and directions, and sets a civil penalty of up to $1,000 per violation, per the Nevada Revised Statutes.
seven_oh_rule: none (statute's definition names 7-OH but sets no 7-OH cap)
pending: none found (Legislature next meets in 2027; no kratom bill found)

status_summary: New Hampshire has no statewide kratom statute that we found. Senate Bill 557, which targeted synthetic and semisynthetic kratom, passed the House but the Senate nonconcurred, and the General Court record lists its status as NONCONCURRED.
seven_oh_rule: none (SB 557 would have banned synthetic or semisynthetic kratom; it failed)
local_action: Merrimack Town Council tabled a draft ordinance on kratom and 7-OH sales (natural leaf exempt for adults 21+) until its Nov. 19, 2026 meeting after an American Kratom Association law firm threatened suit (Union Leader, Nov. 8); Seabrook Planning Board is weighing a synthetic kratom ban for the March 2027 town meeting ballot (WMUR, Oct. 26); Franklin banned kratom in 2019 (WMUR)
pending: Merrimack vote Nov. 19, 2026; Seabrook hearing date not set; 2027 session bills not found

status_summary: New Jersey's Attorney General said on Sept. 25, 2026 that mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15 and MGM-16 became controlled dangerous substances in the state, following the DEA's temporary Schedule I order; the office said natural kratom and unscheduled compounds remain legal.
seven_oh_rule: MGPI, MGM-15 and MGM-16 are state CDS (adopted from DEA temporary order, in place until at least 2028-08-26); concentrated 7-OH itself not separately listed by the state
pending: Bill S4772 (7-OH Schedule I) was reported by a secondary source; not verified

status_summary: We found no New Mexico statewide kratom statute or rule. In December 2025 state environment and health agencies said kratom may not be used in food or drink at state-permitted food establishments, as reported by secondary sources; the state Department of Justice said in November 2025 that no regulations govern kratom products.
seven_oh_rule: none found
local_action: Albuquerque food-permit removals of kratom reported (secondary source, not verified)
pending: none found

status_summary: New York bars kratom sales to anyone under 21 (S4552A/A2340A) and requires a warning label (S8285/A5852A), both signed by Gov. Hochul on Dec. 22, 2025, per the governor's office. A bill banning synthetic kratom, reported passed by both chambers in June, had not been signed as of late October.
seven_oh_rule: Statewide ban on synthetic 7-OH products passed the Legislature in June per the Assembly sponsor (bills A10969/S10514; the Senate site lists them in committee); awaiting governor; sponsor expects signature early 2027
local_action: Nassau, Washington, Oneida (voted Aug. 12, signed late Aug.), Rensselaer (15-2, Sept. 8) and Albany counties ban kratom sales; Dutchess (unanimous Aug. 10, signed Sept.) and Suffolk (vote scheduled July 14, outcome not confirmed) target concentrated or synthetic products; Saratoga committee advanced a full ban Sept. 1; Ulster hearing Nov. 17
pending: State synthetic kratom bill awaits Hochul action; Saratoga Board of Supervisors vote; Ulster County hearing 2026-11-17

status_summary: North Carolina has no enacted statewide kratom statute. House Bill 328, which would ban synthetic kratom and set a 21 age limit, was re-referred to the House Rules Committee on July 30, 2026, and the Speaker said it would get no vote until after the November election (WFAE).
seven_oh_rule: none (HB 328 would add synthetic kratom restrictions; not enacted)
local_action: Dare County approved an ordinance Aug. 3, 2026 limiting sales to 21+, requiring lab testing and capping 7-OH (Island Free Press)
pending: HB 328 returns after the Nov. 2026 election; 2027 session

status_summary: Sales of all kratom remain prohibited in North Dakota until the Attorney General's licensing rules are adopted, the governor's office said on Sept. 4, 2026 when Gov. Armstrong signed HB 1628, which bans synthetic derivatives and sets up licensed natural-leaf sales for adults 21+. His Aug. 3 emergency order was rescinded.
seven_oh_rule: Synthetic kratom derivatives (7-OH, MGM-15, MGM-16, MGPI) banned by HB 1628; natural kratom limited to 0.05% 7-OH dry weight (InForum, KVRR)
pending: AG rulemaking and retailer licensing ($10,000 application fee per KFGO); lawmakers estimated rules could take until March 2027; sales prohibited until then

status_summary: Ohio's Board of Pharmacy rule 4729:9-1-01.1 schedules 7-OH, MGM-15, MGPI and bans kratom extracts, resins, tinctures and (since Aug. 4, 2026) blended products; the Board's Oct. 5, 2026 notice says natural leaf kratom stays legal. A court denied a preliminary injunction against the rule in early August.
seven_oh_rule: 7-OH, MGPI, MGM-15 and 7-acetoxymitragynine Schedule I by rule (emergency Dec. 12, 2025; permanent May 19, 2026); concentrated and processed kratom banned
pending: Botanic Tonics case trial June 2027 (Signal Ohio); whether proposed rule 4729:9-1-01.2 (mitragynine) was adopted is not confirmed

status_summary: Oklahoma's Kratom Consumer Protection Act, as amended by SB 891 (effective Nov. 1, 2025), bars sales under 18, caps 7-OH at 1% of the alkaloid fraction, bans synthesized alkaloids and requires labels and lab-test access. State agencies warned retailers July 13, 2026 about liability for illegal-potency products (KTUL).
seven_oh_rule: 7-OH capped at 1% of alkaloid fraction; synthesized alkaloids banned
pending: Rep. Tim Turner plans a 2027 bill to schedule 7-OH, MGPI and MGM-15 (filing deadline Jan. 14, 2027, session opens Feb. 1); House interim study held Oct. 12, 2026

status_summary: Oregon's Kratom Consumer Protection Act (2022, ORS 475.392 to 475.404) requires processors to register with the Department of Revenue and bars retail sales to anyone under 21 as a Class C misdemeanor, per the Oregon Revised Statutes.
seven_oh_rule: none statewide; a bipartisan group led by Rep. Jules Waters is drafting a 2027 bill that would likely ban concentrated 7-OH (Lund Report)
local_action: Coos County commissioners held a Sept. 30, 2026 work session on a ban for unincorporated areas (KCBY); no vote date reported
pending: Waters bill for 2027 session; Coos County ordinance

status_summary: Pennsylvania has no statewide kratom statute. The House passed HB 2657, a regulation bill that would ban synthetic kratom and set a 21 age limit, 202-0 on Oct. 5, 2026; it was referred to the Senate Health and Human Services Committee Oct. 13, per the General Assembly record.
seven_oh_rule: none statewide; HB 2657 would ban products over 0.5% 7-OH of total alkaloids or over 10 ppm MGPI; Montgomery County DA says concentrated 7-OH is a designer drug under state law (notices Sept. 16)
local_action: Scranton Council voted 5-0 on Oct. 20 for an under-18 kratom ordinance (mayor review pending); Montgomery DA retailer notices Sept. 16; Bucks DA injunction against a Buckingham shop Sept. 2; West Chester sent an ordinance back to committee in August; Philadelphia Council bills outcome not confirmed
pending: HB 2657 in Senate committee; Health Department reviewing DA requests for emergency scheduling (Sept. 8); Scranton mayor decision

status_summary: Under the Rhode Island Kratom Act (R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 21-28.12), in effect April 1, 2026, kratom sales require a state license, sales to anyone under 21 are barred, and products must be kept behind the counter. The Boston Globe reported on July 20 that the state was reviewing manufacturer, importer and distributor applications.
seven_oh_rule: Synthetic alkaloids including synthetic 7-OH banned; products may not exceed 1% 7-OH of total alkaloids, 0.5 mg 7-OH per gram or 1 mg 7-OH per serving (R.I. Gen. Laws 21-28.12-3)
pending: License applications under review (Boston Globe, 2026-07-20); license fees of $2,000 (manufacturer, importer, distributor) and $1,000 (retailer) apply through 2027-12-31, after which the health director sets them by rule; DEA proposed 7-OH scheduling (91 FR 65370, 2026-10-14) pending federally

status_summary: South Carolina regulates kratom under its Kratom Consumer Protection Act (S.C. Code 44-53-2020), which bars sales to anyone under 21 and bans products with fully synthetic alkaloids. H.4641, which would make kratom a Schedule I substance, passed the House 98-4 on April 30, 2026, then stalled in Senate Medical Affairs (WIS-TV, May 11).
seven_oh_rule: Fully synthetic alkaloids, including fully synthetic 7-OH, banned (44-53-2020(A)(2)(c)); no numeric 7-OH cap found
pending: H.4641 (Schedule I for kratom, repeals Article 20) sits in Senate Medical Affairs since 2026-04-30; WIS-TV reported senators plan to study it in the off-season; 2027 pre-filings not yet found

status_summary: South Dakota regulates kratom under 2025 HB 1056 (enrolled text): sales to people under 21 are barred, 7-OH is capped at 2% of alkaloid composition, and violations are Class 2 misdemeanors. 2026 bills to ban kratom failed: SB 77 in the Senate 13-20 on January 22 and HB 1151 in the House 27-39 on February 17, per bill-tracking sources.
seven_oh_rule: 7-OH capped at 2% of alkaloid composition; synthetic derivatives barred (HB 1056 enrolled text)
pending: none found; DEA proposed 7-OH scheduling (91 FR 65370) pending federally

status_summary: Tennessee's ban, Matthew Davenport's Law (HB 1649/SB 1656, Public Chapter 950), was signed May 15, 2026 and took effect July 1, 2026. Possessing kratom is a Class A misdemeanor, and selling or manufacturing it is a felony. The definition covers the plant, extracts and synthetic alkaloids.
seven_oh_rule: Covered by the ban; definition includes 7-OH and synthetically altered alkaloids
pending: Labor commissioner must adopt a rule adding kratom to the workplace drug definition (bill text); enforcement actions continue (Shelby County DA, 2026-10-02; Van Buren County sheriff, 2026-07-22)

status_summary: Texas regulates kratom under the Texas Kratom Consumer Health and Safety Protection Act (2023), which caps 7-OH at 2% of total alkaloids and bars synthetic alkaloids, per the Texas attorney general. The AG sued two California online retailers in April 2026 over products testing 86% to 96% 7-OH.
seven_oh_rule: 7-OH capped at 2% of total alkaloid content; synthetic alkaloids barred
minimum_age: 18 (per RecordingLaw summary of 445.004; statute text not opened)
pending: AG enforcement suits (Smokey's Paradise injunction; Pure Leaf Kratom and Outcast Distribution suit); advocates seeking Schedule I for extracts and a synthetic 7-OH felony ('Jonas's Law') per ABC13, no bill found; 2027 session bills none found

status_summary: Utah's Kratom Adjustments law (S.B. 45), in force May 6, 2026, allows only registered sellers in tobacco specialty shops to sell 'pure leaf kratom', raises the minimum age to 21 and schedules concentrated 7-OH. Botanic Tonics and the Global Kratom Coalition dismissed their federal challenge and Tenth Circuit appeal in late September, after the state approved a pure-leaf product, per FOX 13.
seven_oh_rule: 7-OH above 0.4% of total kratom alkaloids disqualifies a product as pure leaf; 7-OH above a set concentration, including synthetics, and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl scheduled as Schedule I (S.B. 45)
pending: Non-pure-leaf products made in Utah for out-of-state sale permitted until 2027-03-06; litigation ended (dismissed)

status_summary: Vermont bans mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine under state controlled-substance analogues, per the Congressional Research Service (November 2023). Bills H.416 and S.121 to regulate kratom have not advanced; H.416's last action was referral to House Human Services on February 27, 2025. Vermont's own rule text was not located.
seven_oh_rule: Mitragynine and 7-OH both banned
pending: H.416 (House Human Services) and S.121 (Senate Health and Welfare) stalled; 2027 session bills none found

status_summary: Virginia's HB 360, signed by Gov. Abigail Spanberger and in effect July 1, 2026, bars kratom sales to anyone under 21, requires products behind the counter or locked and requires warning labels, and bans products containing 7-OH, per WTVR and Virginia Mercury. WTVR quoted advocates saying more is planned for next year.
seven_oh_rule: Products containing 7-OH banned (HB 360); synthesized material also barred per WTKR
pending: Advocates and sponsor describe HB 360 as a first step; 2027 bills none found; AG Regulated Products Enforcement Unit launched July 30 (Kratom News Today briefing)

status_summary: Washington has no statewide kratom framework, per KIRO 7 (October 28). HB 2291, a Kratom Consumer Protection Act, got a January 30 hearing and remains in the House Consumer Protection and Business Committee. Cities have adopted their own bans.
seven_oh_rule: none (no statewide rule)
local_action: Local sales bans: Mattawa (approved June, effective early August; Kratom News Today briefing), Mount Vernon (2026-08-26), Bellingham (2026-09-14, gross misdemeanor), Spokane and Spokane Valley (dates not confirmed), Arlington (council approved 2026-10-19 per Seattle Times via Kratom News Today briefing); Quincy hearing set for October, outcome not found
pending: Rep. Kristine Reeves plans to reintroduce a Kratom Consumer Protection Act in the 2027 session (KIRO 7, 2026-10-28); HB 2291 never passed

status_summary: West Virginia regulates kratom under the Department of Agriculture's registration regime (W. Va. Code 19-12F). S.B. 985, effective June 12, 2026, requires online sellers to verify buyers are 21 or older and sets felony penalties for selling contaminated product. The law defines kratom products as natural leaf and excludes chemically concentrated products.
seven_oh_rule: No numeric 7-OH cap found; 'kratom product' defined as natural leaf, excluding products synthetically manipulated or chemically concentrated
minimum_age: 21 (online age verification; in-store age not confirmed)
pending: Board of Coal Mine Health and Safety proposed Rule 36-22 adding kratom to prohibited intoxicants at mines, comment closed 2026-10-31 (Kratom News Today briefing, rule page not opened); 2027 bills none found

status_summary: Wisconsin lists mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine in Schedule I of its controlled substances statute (Wis. Stat. 961.14(7)(mk) and (mL)). No 2026 bill to change this was found; Assembly Bill 184 is an unrelated insurance bill.
seven_oh_rule: Mitragynine and 7-OH both Schedule I
pending: none found

status_summary: Wyoming's SF0056 (Enrolled Act 44, Chapter 68), effective July 1, 2026, bars sales to anyone under 21, bans adulterated products, caps 7-OH at 2% of alkaloid composition, and bars candy-like, combustible or vaporizable products. Violations are misdemeanors.
seven_oh_rule: 7-OH capped at 2% of alkaloid composition; synthesized and semi-synthesized alkaloids barred (W.S. 35-7-2202)
pending: Narcotics.com reports Wyoming schedules track federal scheduling unless the AG objects within 30 days, so a final DEA order could flow into state law; governor signing date not confirmed
